extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator; readers interested in taste, aesthetics, and the workings of imagination
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century essay setting out what kinds of visible objects and conditions produce pleasure in the imagination; distinguishes types of imaginative pleasure and lists qualities (greatness, novelty, beauty, etc.) that delight the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Pleasures of the Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Pleasures of the Imagination I mean such as arise from visible Objects, either when we have them actually in our View, or when we call up their Ideas in our Minds by Paintings, Statues, Descriptions, or any the like Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pleasures are originally produced by sight; the essay will use 'fancy' and 'imagination' promiscuously but limits the subject to pleasures arising from sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs Secondary Pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary pleasures entirely proceed from such objects as are before our eyes; secondary pleasures flow from the ideas of visible objects when the objects are not actually before the eye but are called up into memory or formed into agreeable visions of absent or fictitious things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction controls how a work (painting, prospect, description) operates: direct sensory presentation produces primary pleasure, while evocative description or memory produces secondary pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our Senses; it furnishes the Imagination with its ideas and is a more delicate and diffusive kind of touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating imaginative effects, prioritize visual features—sight supplies the raw materials the imagination manipulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure arises from Greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleasures of the Imagination which arise from the actual view proceed from the sight of what is Great ... Greatness includes not only the bulk of a single object but the largeness of a whole view considered as one entire piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expansive horizons, vast landscapes, mountains, wide seas, or any unbounded prospect evoke 'pleasing astonishment' and a sense of liberty; combine greatness with beauty or novelty for stronger effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure arises from Uncommonness/Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that is new or uncommon raises a pleasure in the imagination because it fills the soul with an agreeable surprise, gratifies curiosity, and gives an idea which it was not before possessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty relieves satiety of repeated sights; moving or changing elements (e.g., waterfalls) sustain attention by offering continual newness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure arises from Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing that makes its way more directly to the soul than beauty, which immediately diffuses a secret satisfaction and complacency through the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty may be species-specific (attraction to features of one's own kind) or based on colours, symmetry, proportion, arrangement, and harmonious mixture; immediate, often unanalyzed assent to beauty is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Beauty: species-specific and compositional
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of beauty affects us with the warmest force when it appears in our own species; another kind (in products of art and nature) works by gaiety or variety of colours, symmetry and proportion, arrangement, or mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design beauty either as resonance with innate species preferences (e.g., human form) or as compositional harmony (colour, proportion, arrangement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and Motion enhance pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety is pleasing because the mind is called off to something new; moving elements (rivers, waterfalls) entertain the sight every moment with something new and prevent satiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Static but monotonous scenes tire the eye; incorporate variation and motion to sustain imaginative pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multisensory Enhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any continued sound, as the music of birds, or a fall of water, and fragrances or perfumes heighten the pleasures of the imagination and make colours and verdure appear more agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sound and scent with visual elements to compound pleasures—senses recommend one another and are more pleasant together than separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness preferred to obvious artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of nature are generally more entertaining to the imagination than the works of art; nature exhibits a kind of boldness and immensity art cannot fully replicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that imitate the freedom and variety of nature (seeming 'artless' or accidental) please more than tightly ordered, obviously contrived compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art gains when it resembles Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial works receive advantage from their resemblance to natural ones; when art seems like nature it gives pleasure from both agreeableness and similitude to other objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art by how closely and convincingly it captures natural qualities (including motion and variety); pictures or gardens that mimic nature well afford double pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of formal garden geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: English gardens that show lines, cones, globes, and pyramids (marks of the scissors) are less delightful than plantations that conceal art and present a seeming natural variety; an orchard in flower pleases more than finished parterres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning landscapes or garden scenes, favor naturalistic, varied planting over rigid, geometric trimming; conceal artifice to increase imaginative delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture: greatness in bulk and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness in architecture may be considered either in the bulk and body of the structure or in the manner in which it is built; ancient works often surpassed moderns in bulk and grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For architecture to delight the imagination aim for imposing scale and a manner (design language) that conveys magnitude; both dimensions contribute to the pleasure of grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures as healthful and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of the imagination are not so gross as those of sense, nor so refined as those of the understanding; they are more obvious and easier to acquire and are conducive to health and cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage innocent, imaginal pleasures as safe, restorative entertainments that awaken faculties without taxing them; they are valuable as accessible diversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential negative mixing: horror or loathsomeness
rubrics_metrics.description: An object may be so terrible or offensive that its horror or loathsomeness overbears the pleasure resulting from greatness, novelty, or beauty, though a mixture of delight often remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that extreme terror/loathsomeness can counteract imaginative pleasure; successful works may combine awe with beauty but avoid overwhelming disgust.
